clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its', quotes the film's most famous line so it is instant, and that line is a still title card, not part of the scrolling crawl.
clue1.fix: This 1977 film's laser-blast sound was made by striking the steel guy-wire of a radio tower with a hammer.

clue2.note: Plot summary that gives the answer away at once.
clue2.fix: This film's director took a smaller fee in exchange for the merchandising and sequel rights, which went on to earn billions.

clue3.note: Naming George Lucas and Darth Vader makes it instant.
clue3.fix: In this film, the masked villain was played on set by bodybuilder David Prowse but voiced by James Earl Jones.

clue4.note: Overlaps clue 2's cast of heroes; fine once clue 2 is replaced.

judge.summary: Clues 1 to 3 are all instant (the famous opening line, a plot summary, Lucas and Vader), and clue 1 wrongly says the opening line scrolls.

clue1.note: Plot summary with giveaway words (Kansas, Toto, over the rainbow) in clue 1.
clue1.fix: This movie lost one of its original stars when the aluminum powder in his silver makeup coated his lungs and put him in hospital.

clue2.note: Another plot summary with giveaway names (Dorothy, the yellow brick road).
clue2.fix: This movie's most famous song was nearly cut because studio bosses thought it slowed the opening down.

clue3.note: Opens with an unexplained 'She', is more plot summary, and 'Emerald City' gives it away.
clue3.fix: The actress who played this movie's villain was badly burned when a fire-and-smoke exit effect went off too soon.

judge.summary: Clues 1 to 3 are all plot summary full of giveaway names, so the question is solved instantly on clue 1.

clue1.note: Opens with "The book's" instead of saying the answer is a film.
clue1.fix: This film's magic shoes were silver in the book it was based on; the studio changed their color to show off Technicolor.

clue2.note: A plot summary built on the film's most famous images, so it gives the answer away at once.
clue2.fix: During filming, the actress playing this film's villain was badly burned when the fire effect for her exit went off before she had dropped out of sight.

clue3.note: Another plot summary, opening with a bare "She" and using the giveaway "Emerald City".
clue3.fix: This film's Oscar-winning song was nearly cut because studio bosses thought a ballad sung in a farmyard slowed the picture down.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 are instant plot summaries that repeat the story clue 4 also tells, so the question needs two new facts in the middle and a clue 1 that opens with "This film".

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'its' instead of 'This sport', and the Norway end date of 2014 looks off.
clue1.fix: Sweden banned this sport's professional form in 1970 and kept the ban in place for more than three decades.

clue2.note: Describes how the sport is played and gives it away at once.
clue2.fix: This sport's modern rules are named after a Scottish nobleman, the Marquess of Queensberry, who endorsed them in 1867.

clue3.note: Another description of how bouts work, close to clue 2, and 'knockout' gives it away.
clue3.fix: Women first competed in this sport at the Olympics in London in 2012, the first Games where women took part in every sport on the program.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 are instant descriptions of how the sport works, and clue 1 needs a 'This sport' opening and a checked Norway date.

clue1.note: Repeats clue 4's hundred-dollar-bill and never-president fact.
clue1.fix: As a teenager, this future founder slipped letters into his brother's newspaper under the pen name of a middle-aged widow, Silence Dogood.

clue2.note: The kite experiment is his most famous fact and instant, and he proposed the lightning rod before the kite, not after.
clue2.fix: This founder started Philadelphia's first volunteer fire company and a subscription library that still operates today.

clue4.note: Repeats clue 1; keep this one and rewrite clue 1 instead.

judge.summary: Clue 1 gives away the hundred-dollar bill that clue 4 repeats, and clue 2's kite is instant, so both need lesser-known facts.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare "He" instead of saying the answer is a founder.
clue1.fix: This founder was the only one to sign all four key documents: the Declaration of Independence, the alliance with France, the peace treaty with Britain and the Constitution.

clue2.note: The kite experiment is his most famous story and gives him away at once, and he proposed the lightning rod before the 1752 kite, not after.
clue2.fix: This founder invented a musical instrument of spinning glass bowls, the armonica, and both Mozart and Beethoven wrote music for it.

clue3.note: A list of his roles rather than a fact, and it reuses the Declaration and France from clue 1.
clue3.fix: Writing as "Richard Saunders", this founder published a best-selling yearly almanac that made sayings like "Early to bed and early to rise" famous.

judge.summary: Clue 1 and clue 4 are strong, but clue 2 leads with his best-known story and clue 3 is a resume that repeats clue 1, so both middle clues need fresh, less obvious facts.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its' instead of 'This skyscraper'.
clue1.fix: This skyscraper is so tall that residents on its upper floors are told to break their Ramadan fast a few minutes later than those at street level.

clue2.note: Being the world's tallest building is its defining fact and instant.
clue2.fix: This tower was renamed at its 2010 opening to honor the ruler of Abu Dhabi, the neighboring emirate that had helped bail out its home city.

clue3.note: Naming Dubai on top of the stunt makes it instant.
clue3.fix: Tom Cruise dangled from the outside of this tower, more than 120 floors up, for a 2011 'Mission: Impossible' film.

judge.summary: Clue 1 is a great fact but needs a 'This skyscraper' opening, and clues 2 and 3 are instant because they say 'tallest in the world' and 'Dubai'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and its rise-to-fame idea is repeated in clue 4; it suits clue 2 better.
clue1.fix: This game was made by Innersloth, a three-person studio that shelved its planned sequel in 2020 to keep improving the original.

clue2.note: Describes how the game is played, and 'impostors' gives it away.
clue2.fix: This game sat almost unnoticed for two years after its 2018 release, then exploded in 2020 as streamers picked it up during the pandemic.

clue3.note: Another gameplay description; 'sus' and emergency meetings give it away.
clue3.fix: In 2020 Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez played this game live on Twitch to encourage voting, drawing more than 400,000 viewers.

clue4.note: 'Streaming phenomenon' repeats clue 1's rise to fame.
clue4.fix: This social-deduction game's bean-shaped astronauts must unmask the impostors sabotaging their spaceship.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 both describe the gameplay and are instant, clue 4 repeats clue 1's rise to fame, and clue 1 opens with a bare 'It'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its' instead of 'This observatory's'.
clue1.fix: This observatory's main mirror was ground wrong by about one-fiftieth the width of a human hair, so its first pictures came back blurred.

clue2.note: Continues clue 1's flawed-mirror story, so the two clues share one idea.
clue2.fix: This observatory's 1995 photo of the 'Pillars of Creation' showed towering columns of gas and dust where new stars are forming in the Eagle Nebula.

judge.summary: Strong facts throughout, but clue 1 opens with a bare 'Its' and clue 2 spends a second clue on the same mirror story.

clue1.note: Never says what kind of thing the answer is, and 'enclosed more space than any building' is shakier than the usual 'largest cathedral' claim.
clue1.fix: For nearly a thousand years this domed building was the largest cathedral in the world, until Seville Cathedral overtook it in the 1500s.

clue2.note: Crams three facts (537, the forty windows, the Viking runes) into one long clue.
clue2.fix: A Viking soldier in the Byzantine emperor's guard scratched his name, Halfdan, in runes into a marble railing in this building's upper gallery.

clue4.note: Written as a fragment, not a sentence about the answer.
clue4.fix: This domed church in Istanbul was built for the emperor Justinian, and its Greek name means 'Holy Wisdom'.

judge.summary: Good facts in a good order, but clue 1 has no subject and a doubtful claim, clue 2 crams three facts together, and clue 4 is a fragment.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and 'smallest bone' is its best-known fact, too easy for clue 1.
clue1.fix: This bone can fuse in place and cause hearing loss, and surgeons treat it by swapping it for a tiny artificial piston.

clue3.note: Describes how the bone works rather than giving an interesting fact.
clue3.fix: No bone in the human body is smaller than this one, which is roughly the size of a grain of rice.

clue4.note: Written as a fragment, and 'tiniest' repeats clue 1.
clue4.fix: This middle-ear bone is the third in the chain, after the hammer and the anvil.

judge.summary: Clue 1 leads with the best-known fact (smallest bone) and repeats clue 4, clue 3 only explains how the bone works, and clue 4 is a fragment.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it', and the rotting-meat smell is the source of the nickname clue 4 gives.
clue1.fix: When this plant blooms, it warms itself to near human body temperature to help its scent carry farther.

clue3.note: Its Sumatran origin and giant size are repeated in clue 4; trim clue 4 rather than this one.

clue4.note: Written as a fragment, and 'giant Sumatran' repeats clue 3.
clue4.fix: This plant is nicknamed for the dead-body stench it gives off to lure carrion beetles and flies.

judge.summary: Good facts, but clue 1 opens with a bare 'it' and gives away the smell, and clue 4 is a fragment that repeats clue 3.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and the Oscar record is the film's best-known fact, easier than clues 2 and 3.
clue1.fix: A dish in this film that mixes two brands of instant noodles became so famous that sales of both brands soared worldwide.

clue2.note: Plot summary rather than a fact.
clue2.fix: This film won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2019, the first Korean film to take the festival's top prize.

clue3.note: A vague plot teaser about the basement, not a fact.
clue3.fix: This South Korean film became the first not in English to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 are plot summary, and the Oscar record in clue 1 is the best-known fact, so it belongs in clue 3.

clue1.note: Instant, and relativity rests on this being the same for every observer; the speed limit follows from that.
clue1.fix: This constant was first estimated in 1676, when Ole Romer noticed that eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io ran late whenever Earth was farther from Jupiter.

clue2.note: Repeats the 'ultimate limit' idea of clues 1 and 4 and is instant.
clue2.fix: Since 1983 the meter has been defined by this constant, as the distance it covers in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

clue3.note: Nearly all stars visible to the eye are close enough that they still exist, so the 'may have died' idea is misleading.
clue3.fix: Because of this constant, we see the Sun as it was about eight minutes ago.

clue4.note: 'Cosmic top speed' repeats clue 2; fine once clue 2 is replaced.

judge.summary: Three clues rest on the same 'nothing is faster' idea and clue 1 is instant, so the question needs new facts for clues 1 to 3.

clue1.note: Never says 'this game'; its subject is the studio, so it does not say what the answer is.
clue1.fix: This game's mythology was written by the author of A Song of Ice and Fire, for a studio famous for punishing difficulty.

clue3.note: A dry list of credits that names the studio clue 1 hinted at.
clue3.fix: This game beat God of War Ragnarok to win Game of the Year at The Game Awards in 2022.

clue4.note: Uses 'Elden', a word from the answer's name.
clue4.fix: In this FromSoftware open-world epic, players called the Tarnished set out to repair a shattered relic and claim the throne.

judge.summary: Clue 4 uses 'Elden' from the answer's name, and clue 1 is about the studio rather than 'this game'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it' instead of 'This sport'.
clue1.fix: Three fathers on Washington's Bainbridge Island made up this sport in 1965 to entertain their bored families.

clue2.note: 'Fastest-growing sport' is its best-known fact and an 'it is popular' clue.
clue2.fix: Neighbors in some U.S. towns have sued over this sport because of the loud pop of its hard paddles.

clue4.note: Written as a fragment, not a sentence about the answer.
clue4.fix: This paddle sport, often said to be named after a family dog, mixes elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis.

judge.summary: Clue 2's 'fastest-growing sport' is instant and comes before a harder clue 3, clue 1 needs 'This sport', and clue 4 is a fragment.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its' instead of 'This print's'.
clue1.fix: This print's striking blue came from Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment newly imported to Japan from Europe.

clue4.note: Written as a fragment, not a sentence about the answer.
clue4.fix: This Japanese print shows a towering, claw-tipped breaker about to crash down on three fishing boats.

judge.summary: Four distinct facts in a good order; only clue 1's bare 'Its' and clue 4's fragment need fixing.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its' and is a plot episode, like clue 2.
clue1.fix: This epic gave English the word 'mentor', from the old friend whose form the goddess Athena takes to guide the hero's son.

clue2.note: A list of plot episodes from the same voyage as clue 1.
clue2.fix: James Joyce modeled his 1922 novel about a single day in Dublin on this epic, and named the novel after its hero's Latin name.

clue3.note: Naming Homer and Odysseus gives it away at once.
clue3.fix: Attributed to Homer, this epic ends with its hero returning home in disguise and killing the suitors who courted his wife.

judge.summary: Clues 1 and 2 are plot episodes from the same voyage and clue 3 names Odysseus, so three clues need new facts.
